subject: Covariate estimates in occupancy vs N-mixture models

messages.author: 9743508ad656e4da
messages.subject: Covariate estimates in occupancy vs N-mixture models
parts:
Hi all,

I am investigating the relative abundance of reptile species across multiple savanna vegetation communities using data from a time-to-detection survey. Although abundance is the operative word here, and thus I will focus on using N-mixture models, I am curious why I am getting vastly different estimates of covariate effects when running occuTTD() versus nmixTTD().

For example, here the occupancy of a predominantly arboreal lizard is modelled as a product of variation in the dominance of an invasive tree species (i.e., % of the tree canopy dominated by the invasive), with three detection covariates, using occuTTD():



And the same combination of covariates when run with nmixTTD() yields:



Similarly, transforming the data to a DND matrix and running the traditional occu() yields:



While running occuRN() yields:



My question is why would both occupancy models have much more uncertain estimates than either of the N-mixture models?

Thank you in advance,

Kurt

messages.author: 4a15de51da4445ae
messages.subject: Re: Covariate estimates in occupancy vs N-mixture models
parts:
hi Kurt,
 The first set of results you show from occuTTD indicate that model parameters are not identifiable due to (most likely) the naive occupancy rate being 1. i.e., all of your sites have detections at them. Thus there is no variation in occurrence to model.  
regards
andy

Thanks for your response. The naive occupancy was 0.76. The species was not detected at 4 of the 21 sites, and each site was surveyed 5 times. More complex models also provide similar estimates with large SE and P(>|z|) = 1.000 for all environmental covariates.
